title: Passive III: s-passive, bli or vara?
title_target: Allt måste vara klart i morgon kväll.
goal: Choose between the three Swedish passives — *skickas*, *blev stulen*, *är låst* — use the passive after modal verbs, and know when to drop the passive altogether in favor of *man*.
bekal: you can form the s-passive in every tense and after modals (*måste skickas*, *har godkänts*)
you can tell an event (*blev stulen*) from a state (*är låst*) and make the participle agree
you can turn a stiff passive into everyday Swedish with *man* or *vi*
wave: Go back to Unit 9: take ten past participles from it and give all three forms of each (*stängd – stängt – stängda*, *skriven – skrivet – skrivna*) — you'll need every one of them with *är* and *blev* in this unit.

notes: **ska lanseras** (**skah lahn-SEH-rahs**) — after a modal verb, the passive is simply the infinitive + *-s*: *ska lanseras*, *måste skickas*, *får göras*, *ska testas*, *brukar göras*. This is by far the most common passive in working life — every to-do list, email and meeting is full of it.

**Texterna är redan skrivna** — *vara* + participle describes a **state** or result: the texts are written, done, ready. Compare *bilderna har inte godkänts*, which is about the **action** (approving) that hasn't happened yet. The participle agrees like an adjective: *texten är skriven*, *brevet är skrivet*, *texterna är skrivna*.

**har ändrats, godkändes, har godkänts** — the s-passive works in every tense. Past: add *-s* to the past form (*godkände* → *godkändes*). Perfect: *har* + supine + *-s* (*har godkänt* → *har godkänts*, pronounced **GOOD-shents**).

**Den blev aldrig färdig. Leila blev sjuk.** — *bli* + adjective means "to get, to become": a **change** of state. It's not a passive, but it's the same pattern you'll use for the *bli*-passive in the next dialogue: *blev färdig*, *blev sjuk*, *blev stulen*.

**menyn får göras av någon annan** — *få* + passive here means "will have to be", not "may be": the job lands on someone else. The person who does the action, if you mention them at all, is introduced with **av**: *godkänts **av** kunden*, *görs **av** någon annan*.

**Ska jag kontaktas?** — Mattias is teasing Karin: a passive about yourself, with *ska*, is pure official style, the kind of Swedish you'll find in letters from authorities. Karin switches to everyday Swedish at once: *ring mig*. And **krångla** (**KRONG-lah**) is the perfect word for technology that misbehaves: *Datorn krånglar igen.*

grammars.title: The s-passive in every tense
body: Take the active form and add **-s**. In the present tense, the *-er* ending drops first (*skriver* → *skrivs*); a stem that already ends in *-s* adds *-es* (*läser* → *läses*).

head: Tense
Active
s-passive
rows: har skickat · har skrivit · har gjort
har skickat**s** · har skrivit**s** · har gjort**s**
måste skicka · ska skriva · får göra
måste skicka**s** · ska skriva**s** · får göra**s**

after: Strong verbs follow their own forms: *stjäla – stjäls – stals – har stulits*, *ta – tas – togs – har tagits*, *se – ses – sågs – har setts*.
With a particle verb, the *-s* goes on the verb and the particle stays behind it: *klippa upp* → *låset klipptes upp*, *ställa in* → *mötet har ställts in*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Cykeln blev stulen
dialogs.intro: The following Monday. Dian arrives at the office forty minutes late and out of breath. Leila, back from being sick, is the first to see her.

lines.text: Varför är du så sen? Du brukar ju alltid komma först.

notes: **Min cykel har blivit stulen** — the **bli-passive** (*bli* + participle) tells about an **event**, often something that happens *to* someone, unexpected or unwelcome. It's more common in speech than in writing. *Stulen* comes from the strong verb *stjäla* (**HWEH-lah**: *stjäl – stal – stulit*) and agrees: *cykeln blev stulen*, *ett lås blev stulet*, *cyklarna blev stulna*.

**Var den inte låst? — Jo, den var låst.** — *vara* + participle again describes the **state**: the bike was in a locked state. *Jo* is the "yes" that contradicts a negative question, as you learned in Svenska 101.

**låset hade klippts upp** — the pluperfect s-passive: *hade* + supine + *-s*. The particle (*upp*) stays after the verb. As an adjective, the same verb fuses with its particle: *ett uppklippt lås* (Unit 7).

**Det stjäls tusentals cyklar** (**deh hwels TÜ-sen-tahls SÜK-lahr**) — Unit 12's empty *det* combines with the s-passive: *det* + passive verb + an indefinite subject. *Det byggs mycket i Göteborg* (There's a lot of building going on in Göteborg). *Det sägs att…* (It's said that…).

**det görs enkelt på nätet** — the s-passive is the natural way to describe routines and procedures: *Hur görs det?* (How is it done?). **Anmäla** (**AHN-meh-lah**) means to report something to an authority; the report itself is *en polisanmälan*.

**Ofta ingår cykeln** — English "is included" is a passive, but Swedish uses the **active** verb *ingå* (**IN-goh**): *Frukost ingår* (Breakfast is included). Don't translate every English passive into a Swedish one — and **höra av sig** (to get in touch) is another active phrase English renders differently.

grammars.title: Three passives — which one when?
body: All three exist side by side, and they are not interchangeable. Ask yourself: is this a **process or routine**, a single **event**, or a **state**?

head: Form
Typical meaning
Example
rows: process, routine, rule, instruction; neutral and written; always after modals
a single event, a change, often unexpected; more spoken

after: A quick test: if you can add "already" and mean "it's in that state now", use *vara*: *Texterna är (redan) skrivna.* If you're telling what happened, use the s-passive or *bli*: *Texterna skrevs i går* / *Texterna blev skrivna i går*.
With verbs of feeling or reaction, *bli* is the only choice: *Jag blev förvånad* (I was surprised), *Hon blev glad*, *Vi blev inbjudna* (we got invited). Using the s-passive there sounds odd.

grammars.title: Avoiding the passive: man, vi, active verbs
body: In everyday speech, Swedes often avoid the passive altogether. The pronoun **man** (one, you, people) carries the same impersonal meaning without sounding like an authority. Swedish plain-language guidelines (*klarspråk*) recommend exactly this for official texts too.

blocks.text: With *vara* and *bli*, the participle behaves like an adjective: it agrees with the subject in gender and number. These are the forms you'll use most often in this unit.

Notice the particle verbs at the bottom: as participles, the particle moves **in front** and fuses with the verb — *ställa in* → *inställd*, *bjuda in* → *inbjuden*. In the s-passive it stays behind: *mötet ställdes in*.

blocks.title: Signs you'll see everywhere
items: **Stängt** — Closed (the neuter form, because it describes the situation, like *det är stängt*).
**Rökning förbjuden** — No smoking. **Obehöriga äga ej tillträde** — Authorized personnel only (an old-fashioned formula with a plural verb that survives on doors).
**Varorna betalas i kassan** — Pay for your goods at the checkout.

blocks.text: Bike theft is a fact of life in Swedish cities. Most people have a **hemförsäkring** (home insurance), which usually covers your belongings — including a bike — whether you rent or own. You pay a **självrisk** (deductible) yourself, and the insurance company needs a police report number before it pays anything.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Svenska 102, Units 5 and 6
items: Read five signs or notices around you (or on a Swedish website) and find every *-s* passive.
Turn each one into an active sentence with *man*: *Kaffet serveras kl. 8* → *Man serverar kaffet kl. 8*.
Then describe three things in your home with *är* + participle: *Fönstret är stängt*, *Lampan är tänd*, *Böckerna är sorterade*.
